title: HTTP & TLS
description: Methods, status codes, caching, HTTP/2, certificates and CORS.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is intended to replace a resource entirely and is idempotent?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces the target resource with the request body, and repeating it gives the same result. POST is not idempotent and PATCH is a partial update.

questions.prompt: What does the 301 status code mean?
questions.explanation: 301 tells clients and search engines the resource has permanently moved. 302 (and 307) are temporary redirects, 304 is 'not modified'.

questions.prompt: A user is signed in but tries to open an admin page they may not see. Which status is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: 403 means the server understood who you are and refuses access. 401 (despite its name) means 'not authenticated'.

questions.prompt: Which of these HTTP headers influence caching? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Cache-Control sets freshness and rules, and ETag enables conditional revalidation. Set-Cookie and Accept-Language don't control caching directly.

questions.prompt: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve compared with HTTP/1.1?
choices: Many requests share one connection without waiting for each other at the HTTP level
It removes the need for DNS
It makes responses smaller by default
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 needed multiple connections or queued requests. HTTP/2 interleaves streams on one connection. TCP-level head-of-line blocking remains, which is what HTTP/3 addresses.

questions.prompt: What are the two main goals of the TLS handshake?
choices: Authenticate the server and agree on shared session keys
Resolve the hostname and open a port
Assign an IP address and gateway
questions.explanation: TLS authenticates the server (via its certificate) and derives symmetric session keys so the rest of the traffic can be encrypted efficiently.

questions.prompt: What does a certificate signed by a trusted CA actually tell the browser?
choices: The CA vouches that this public key belongs to this domain
The server is free of vulnerabilities
The connection will never be intercepted
questions.explanation: A certificate binds a public key to a domain name, vouched for by a CA the browser trusts. It says nothing about whether the site itself is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A browser blocks a cross-origin fetch with a CORS error. Who has to change something for it to work?
choices: The server being called, by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin
questions.explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser but configured by the server. The response must include headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin that allow the calling origin.
